source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει· καί ποτε προαγαγεῖν βουληθεὶς αὐτοὺς περὶ τῶν ἀρχαίων εἰς λόγους τῶν τῇδε τῇ πόλει τὰ ἀρχαιότατα λέγειν ἐπιχειρεῖ, περὶ Φορωνέως τε τοῦ πρώτου λεχθέντος καὶ Νιόβης, καὶ τὰ μετὰ τὸν κατακλυσμόν. κατὰ δὲ Φόρβαντα Ἀκταῖος, ἀφ’ οὗ Ἀκταία ἡ Ἀττική. κατὰ δὲ Τριόπαν Προμηθεὺς καὶ Ἄτλας καὶ Ἐπιμηθεὺς καὶ ὁ διφυὴς Κέκροψ καὶ Ἰώ. κατὰ δὲ Κρότωπον ἡ ἐπὶ Φαέθοντος ἐκπύρωσις καὶ ἡ ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος ἐπομβρία. κατὰ δὲ Σθένελον ἥ τε Ἀμφικτυόνος βασιλεία καὶ ἡ εἰς Πελοπόννησον Δαναοῦ παρουσία καὶ ἡ ὑπὸ Δαρδάνου τῆς Δαρδανίας κτίσις, ὃν πρῶτον, φησὶν Ὅμηρος, τέκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς, ἥ τε τῆς Εὐρώπης εἰς Κρήτην ἐκ Φοινίκης ἀνακομιδή. κατὰ δὲ Λυγκέα τῆς κόρης ἡ ἁρπαγὴ καὶ ἡ τοῦ ἐν Ἐλευσῖνι τεμένους καθίδρυσις Τριπτολέμου τε γεωργία καὶ ἡ Κάδμου εἰς Θήβας παρουσία Μίνωός τε βασιλεία. κατὰ δὲ Προῖτον ὁ Εὐμόλπου πρὸς Ἀθηναίους πόλεμος. κατὰ δὲ Ἀκρίσιον Πέλοπος ἀπὸ Φρυγίας διάβασις καὶ Ἴωνος εἰς Ἀθήνας ἄφιξις καὶ ὁ δεύτερος Κέκροψ αἵ τε Περσέως καὶ Διονύσου πράξεις Ὀρφεύς τε καὶ Μουσαῖος. κατὰ δὲ τὸ ὀκτωκαιδέκατον ἔτος τῆς Ἀγαμέμνονος βασιλείας Ἴλιον ἑάλω, Δημοφῶντος τοῦ Θησέως βασιλεύοντος Ἀθήνησι τῷ πρώτῳ ἔτει, θαργηλιῶνος μηνὸς δευτέρᾳ ἐπὶ δέκα, ὥς φησι Διονύσιος ὁ Ἀργεῖος, Ἀγίας δὲ καὶ Δερκύλος ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ μηνὸς πανήμου ὀγδόῃ φθίνοντος, Ἑλλάνικος γὰρ δωδεκάτῃ θαργηλιῶνος μηνός. καί τινες τῶν τὰ Ἀττικὰ συγγραψαμένων ὀγδόῃ φθίνοντος, βασιλεύοντος τὸ τελευταῖον ἔτος Μενεσθέως, πληθυούσης σελήνης·
pass_a_gloss: And concerning the fact that the doctrines of the philosophers were seen by the Hebrews, we will speak a little later, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Now, Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, who was called Plistonices, in the fourth of his Egyptian histories, although he was disposed in a rather hostile manner towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and having even composed a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, the king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and he presents Ptolemaeus of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king according to the Argive Inachus, dug up Auaria, as Ptolemaeus of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now, this Ptolemaeus was a priest, and in three whole books, he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he says that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their departure from Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. And of these, the Attic, which are from Cecrops, the double-born and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger. And the Arcadic, which are from Pelasgus, are nine generations younger; and this one is also said to be autochthonous. And of these, the Phthiotic, which are from Deucalion, are two generations younger. Now, going back to the time of the Trojan War from Inachus, twenty or a few more generations are counted, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if the things of the Assyrians are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be shown that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Beluchus, the departure of Moses from Egypt, according to Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, took place. Now, in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there was the flood of Ogyges and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man; hence, the poet of the Phoroneis says that he was the father of mortal men. From this, Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus: and at some point, wanting to lead them on to discussions about the ancient things of this city, he attempts to speak about the most ancient things, about Phoroneus, who was said to be the first, and about Niobe, and about the things after the flood. Now, according to Phorbas, Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea comes, and according to Triopas, Prometheus and Atlas and Epimetheus and the double-born Cecrops and Io. And according to Crotopus, the conflagration of Phaethon and the flood of Deucalion. And according to Sthenelus, the kingdom of Amphictyon and the arrival of Danaus in Peloponnese and the foundation of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, and the migration of Europe from Phoenicia to Crete. And according to Lynceus, the abduction of his daughter and the establishment of the temple in Eleusis, and the agriculture of Triptolemus, and the arrival of Cadmus in Thebes, and the kingdom of Minos. And according to Proetus, the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians. And according to Acrisius, the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia and the arrival of Ion in Athens, and the second Cecrops, and the deeds of Perseus and Dionysus, and Orpheus and Musaeus. And in the eighteenth year of the reign of Agamemnon, Ilion was taken, in the first year of the reign of Demophon, son of Theseus, in Athens, on the second day of the month of Thargelion, as Dionysius of Argos says, and on the eighth day of the month of Panemus, as Agias and Dercylus say, when the moon was full, for Hellanicus says it was on the twelfth day of the month of Thargelion.

pass_b_english: We will take up a little later the question of whether the philosophers' doctrines were derived from the Hebrews; first, as the sequence demands, we must speak of the times of Moses, through which it will be shown beyond dispute that Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his Address to the Greeks, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his Exegetical Notes; nevertheless, this memorandum also requires us to run through the statements relevant to our subject. Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonices, in the fourth book of his Egyptian Histories — though he writes with marked hostility toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth and having even composed a work against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and he cites Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's words run thus: "Amosis destroyed Avaris when Inachus was reigning in Argos, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his Chronicles." This Ptolemy was a priest; in three full books he set out the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he states that under Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews made their departure from Egypt under the leadership of Moses, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of the Greek traditions are the Argive, which begin with Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. Of these, the Attic line from Cecrops the double-born and autochthonous — as Tatian puts it word for word — is forty generations younger; the Arcadian line from Pelasgus is nine generations younger, and Pelasgus is also said to be autochthonous; the Phthiotic line from Deucalion is two generations younger still. Counting back from Inachus to the Trojan War, one reckons twenty or a few more generations, and, so to speak, four hundred years. But if Assyrian history is many years older than Greek history, as Ctesias says, then the departure of Moses from Egypt under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive will be seen to fall in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire and the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus.

In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who succeeded Inachus, the flood of Ogyges occurred, along with the kingdom in Sicyon — first Aegialeus, then Europs, then Telchin — and the reign of Cydas in Crete. Acusilaus declares that Phoroneus was the first man; hence the poet of the Phoroneid calls him the father of mortal men. Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus that, wishing to draw them into talk of the most ancient things of this city, he begins with Phoroneus, who was said to be first, with Niobe, and with what came after the flood. Under Phorbas comes Actaeus, from whom the Attic Acte takes its name. Under Triopas come Prometheus, Atlas, Epimetheus, the double-born Cecrops, and Io. Under Crotopus come the conflagration of Phaethon and the flood of Deucalion. Under Sthenelus come the kingdom of Amphictyon, the arrival of Danaus in the Peloponnese, the founding of Dardania by Dardanus — whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus — and the carrying of Europa from Phoenicia to Crete. Under Lynceus come the abduction of his daughter, the establishment of the sanctuary at Eleusis, the agriculture of Triptolemus, the arrival of Cadmus in Thebes, and the reign of Minos. Under Proetus comes the war of Eumolpus against the Athenians. Under Acrisius come the crossing of Pelops from Phrygia, the arrival of Ion in Athens, the second Cecrops, the deeds of Perseus and Dionysus, and the figures of Orpheus and Musaeus.

In the eighteenth year of Agamemnon's reign Troy was taken; in the first year of Demophon son of Theseus as king of Athens, on the second day of the month Thargelion according to Dionysius of Argos, on the eighth day of the waning moon in the month Panemus according to Agias and Dercylus, when the moon was full — for Hellanicus says the twelfth day of Thargelion — and some of the Attic chroniclers place it on the eighth day of the waning moon in the last year of Menestheus' reign.

review.notes: Pass B fails on completeness and accuracy regarding the final sentence. The Greek text ends with 'πληθυούσης σελήνης·' (the moon being full/increasing), whereas Pass B translates this as 'the waning moon' ('the eighth day of the waning moon in the month Panemus... when the moon was full'). While the Greek 'φθίνοντος' (waning) appears earlier in the sentence regarding the month of Panemus, the final clause 'πληθυούσης σελήνης' refers to the moon being full/waxing, which Pass B contradicts by grouping it with the waning moon description. Additionally, Pass B omits the final clause of the Greek text: 'βασιλεύοντος τὸ τελευταῖον ἔτος Μενεσθέως, πληθυούσης σελήνης·' is partially rendered but the relationship between the moon's phase and the reign of Menestheus is muddled compared to the Greek structure.
reasons: Pass B contradicts the Greek 'πληθυούσης σελήνης' (the moon being full/waxing) by describing the timing as 'the waning moon' in a way that creates a logical contradiction within the sentence structure, and fails to precisely capture the final clause's relationship to the moon's phase.
